stem: A client who uses subcutaneous insulin reports repeatedly injecting into the same thickened, lumpy area because the injections feel less painful there. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Stop injecting into the abnormal area, rotate sites within an appropriate region, and monitor glucose more closely when changing to unaffected tissue.
options.B: Continue using the lumpy area because lipodystrophy improves insulin absorption and reduces glucose variability.
options.C: Massage the thickened area immediately after each injection so insulin enters the bloodstream more rapidly.
options.D: Use only the same exact skin spot for each dose because changing sites is the main cause of lipodystrophy.

rationale: A is correct. Current insulin labeling instructs clients to rotate injection sites to reduce lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis and to avoid injecting into areas that are thickened, pitted, or lumpy. Repeated injections into affected tissue have been associated with hyperglycemia, while a sudden change from affected to unaffected tissue can increase the risk of hypoglycemia; closer glucose monitoring is therefore appropriate during the change. B and D reverse the purpose of site rotation. C is not a recommended strategy for correcting abnormal injection-site tissue and introduces unpredictable absorption rather than addressing the cause.
educational_objective: Teach insulin users to avoid lipodystrophic or lumpy injection areas, rotate injection sites appropriately, and monitor glucose closely when moving injections from affected to unaffected tissue because insulin absorption may change.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration
source_locator: Dosage and Administration, Section 2.1 — rotate sites within the same region to reduce lipodystrophy/localized cutaneous amyloidosis and avoid affected skin; Warnings and Precautions — repeated injections into affected areas reported with hyperglycemia and sudden change to unaffected areas reported with hypoglycemia
source_claim_supported: Insulin injection sites should be rotated and abnormal lipodystrophic/amyloid areas avoided; moving from chronically affected tissue to unaffected tissue can alter insulin effect and requires closer glucose monitoring.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; safely administer parenteral medications, evaluate response, and educate clients about injection technique
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin injection-site rotation and lipodystrophy
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source recall question into a clinical teaching scenario and corrected the blueprint from infection control to Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies. The final version adds the current FDA warning that switching from chronically affected tissue to normal tissue can increase hypoglycemia risk and should prompt closer glucose monitoring.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current FDA/DailyMed insulin labeling. Rotation prevents lipodystrophy/localized cutaneous amyloidosis, and affected tissue should not be used for injection.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A includes only label-supported site avoidance, rotation, and closer monitoring during a change to unaffected tissue. The rationale avoids asserting that absorption is always increased or decreased in every lesion.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; matches current injection-site and monitoring guidance.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; affected tissue is associated with unreliable glycemic effect, not improved absorption.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; massage is not the labeled corrective action for lipodystrophy and may alter absorption.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; repeated use of the same site contributes to the problem rather than preventing it.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A addresses both the abnormal tissue and the glycemic risk of changing sites.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are injection-technique teaching actions of comparable scope.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies is the correct primary category because the construct is safe subcutaneous insulin administration, not infection prevention.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked lipodystrophy versus localized amyloidosis, site-rotation wording, hyperglycemia/hypoglycemia transition risk, massage claim, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
